item.title: Developer turns to back-contact module tech for NSW solar project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Back-contact solar modules supplied by Longi will be used exclusively in a bid to maximise energy yield at a 135 MW solar farm being built at the site of a former coal mine in the New South Wales Hunter Valley.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese PV manufacturer Longi has been tapped to supply about 300,000 solar modules featuring its next-generation back-contact (BC) cell technology to developer OX2 for its Muswellbrook solar-plus-storage hybrid project in the New South Wales (NSW) Upper Hunter region.

Construction has already commenced on the hybrid project being built by Swedish-headquartered OX2 in partnership with the Australian arm of Japanese resources and energy company Idemitsu. The $302 million (USD 203 million) project includes a 135 MW (176 MWdc) solar farm and a 100 MW / 200 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) deployed across a 482-hectare site adjacent to the now-shuttered Muswellbrook coal mine, owned by Idemitsu.

The solar facility is being equipped with Longi’s Hi-MO 9 bifacial PV modules that are powered by the company’s hybrid passivated back-contact cell technology and Tairay silicon wafers.

Longi said the Hi-MO 9 series represent “a massive leap forward in utility-scale solar technology,” with module efficiencies of up to 24.8% helping to maximise energy yield in Australia’s harsh climate and high-irradiance conditions.

“Supplying our flagship Hi-MO 9 modules to this project proves the market’s deep trust in Longi’s technological leadership, and product reliability,” Longi Utility Europe President Leon Zhang said.

“Our back-contact technology is uniquely designed to deliver maximum energy yield and long-term value, even in challenging environments.”

Longi said the Hi-MO 9 modules feature a zero-busbar front-side design, temperature coefficient of -0.26%/°C, and a 30-year power warranty with annual degradation 0.05 percentage points lower than standard N-type products.

Compared to TOPCon modules, Longi said its Hi-MO 9 series deliver a 1.5% absolute efficiency gain, and increases installed capacity by approximately 6.4% over equivalent land area. 

Once operational, the Muswellbrook PV plant is projected to generate about 347 GWh of clean electricity annually. 

France-headquartered contractors Bouygues Construction, through its subsidiary Bouygues Construction Australia, and Equans, through Equans Solar & Storage,  are delivering the solar project under an engineering, procurement and construction contract.

Construction commenced on the project in May 2026, with full commissioning and grid connection expected in 2028.

e-Storage, the energy storage-focused subsidiary of PV giant Canadian Solar, has been contracted to supply and commission the 100 MW / 200 MWh BESS.

item.title: ClearVue secures solar cladding supply deal for Singapore project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Perth-based building-integrated PV specialist ClearVue Technologies has secured a contract to supply 4,000 square metres of solar cladding, with a designed capacity of about 670 kWp, for a government building in Singapore.
item.content:encoded:
ClearVue Technologies has received a letter of award (LOA) for a sub-contract worth up to almost $860,000 to supply its energy-generating solar cladding technology for a Singapore government-owned building in the city-state.

The contract, valued at between $573,000 to $859,800 (SGD 500,000 and 750,000) and awarded through an unidentified Singapore-based façade contractor, covers approximately 4,000 square metres of façade area on the building.

ClearVue said it will manufacture and supply solar energy-generating laminated glass panels, finished in grey with matching aluminium edge framing, for the project. The system has been designed to deliver a combined 670 kW of electricity generation capacity, contributing to the building’s overall annual renewable energy target.

The company said it will also manufacture bespoke framing for the project and will utilise its thermal bridge junction box technology on a sealed-face façade, the specific application the technology was designed for.

While unable to name the contractor or the specific project due to commercial confidentiality, ClearVue Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Doug Hunt said the contract is “strong commercial validation” of the company’s technology.

“Being selected to supply a government project in Singapore is a significant achievement, not just for this project, but for the business we have spent years building,” he said, adding that the importance goes well beyond the value of this project in revenue.

“We are taking Australian-developed technology into international government infrastructure,” he said. “That is a substantial commercial milestone and strengthens our credibility as we pursue major projects across Asia and around the world.”

The LOA remains subject to project design approvals and final approvals of the manufacturing plan. Final contract value will reflect quantities supplied and delivered.

This latest contract adds to ClearVue’s growing list of projects. It follows a contract to supply its building-integrated PV glazing for a 169 kW project in Cyprus, and a $600,000 subcontract to supply and install its solar products at Canva’s new global headquarters in Sydney.

Earlier this month, ClearVue secured a $712,450 (USD 500,000) grant from the United States Department of Energy (DOE) to accelerate its push into the American market.

In partnership with North American solar manufacturer Silfab Solar, the company will use the funds to advance its spandrel technology. The grant will support technical development of the technology, performance validation, and evaluation of viable US manufacturing pathways.

ClearVue has also recently established an office and showroom in Hong Kong to support its growth ambitions in the region.

item.title: Clarifying CATL Tener Sodium, with new specifications and availability
item.dc:creator: Tristan Rayner
item.description: New specs for CATL’s four-hour sodium-ion battery reveal how the company will market the product for cost benefits over LFP-based batteries. International deliveries are due to begin in summer 2027.
item.content:encoded:
CATL’s Tener Sodium battery energy storage system (BESS) is one of the most anticipated new products on the market, as markets watch for the great hope to compete with lithium-ion products across a number of potential scenarios.

The Tener Sodium product launched at The Smarter E event 2026 in Munich in June, and at the time, the company gave a capacity of more than 30 MWh per block.

With further details scarce, an Oct. 29 ATA Insights webinar featuring CATL energy storage product solution manager David Santiago showed specifications and datasheets across the BESS and in-house PCS to detail how the four-hour system comes together.

The system is built in pairs, with two, four, six or eight cabinets available to spec. The full block sits in two back-to-back rows of four and measures 18.2 m across, 7 m deep and 3.5 m high.

Santiago put each cabinet at about 4.5 metres (15 feet) long and 44 to 45 metric tons. That works out to about 4 MWh per cabinet in the eight-cabinet version.

At launch, CATL had put the module weight at about 42 metric tons. CATL also plans to use the same cabinets and layout for a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) version. Santiago put that version at about 50 MWh across eight cabinets and said developers could choose the chemistry during project design. CATL is prioritising sodium-ion certification, with the LFP version to follow.

Tener Sodium: Core battery specs

The provided system specifications lists a rated energy of 30+ MWh, with a charge and discharge rate of up to 0.25P, or a power output of 7.5 MW for four hours. (Santiago didn’t specify a power output change if the block has a final capacity of 32 MWh).

The battery is rated at 1,166.88 V DC, with a voltage range of 612 V to 1,387.2 V. CATL specifies 95% round-trip efficiency at 25°C and 0.25P, and 70% state of health after 20 years under a 0.25P duty cycle marked “1cls” on the slide.

The liquid-cooled battery operates from −35°C to +55°C and can be stored from −35°C to +60°C. CATL lists noise at 65 dB(A) or less, IP55 ingress protection, C5 corrosion protection with C4 optional, and operation up to 4,000 m without derating. Communications include CAN, Modbus TCP/IP and RS485.

At launch, CATL reported 15,000 cycles at 25°C and more than 10,000 at 45°C, as well as more than 92% capacity retention at −20°C. The liquid-cooled battery operates from −35°C to +55°C. It is rated IP55, with operation up to 4,000 m without derating.

PCS: CATL’s own in-house Terapower 265 kW converter

CATL uses bidirectional DC/DC conversion to boost voltage at the low end of the battery’s range. The Terapower module shown in the webinar combines that DC/DC stage with a power conversion system (PCS). CATL offers its own PCS though it can also work with other manufacturers.

It takes 600 V to 1,500 V DC at up to 222 A and is rated at 265 kW, with a 690 V AC output at 50 or 60 Hz. CATL lists peak efficiency of at least 99.2%, full-load efficiency of at least 98.5% and current harmonic distortion below 3% at rated load.

The converter is liquid-cooled and rated IP66, with an operating range of −40°C to +60°C and a maximum altitude of 5,000 m. It starts to derate above 50°C and above 3,000 m. It lists RS485, Ethernet and CAN interfaces and support for IEC 61850 and Modbus TCP.

Santiago said the PCS ties into the battery’s thermal management system and is accounted for in its auxiliary consumption.

Tener Sodium cooling, auxiliary power, cycling vs CATL’s LFP EnerX

Against its EnerX 0.25P LFP system, CATL says the sodium-ion cells generate 27.2% less heat per unit of energy at the beginning of life and 32.7% less at end of life.

For a 50 MWh station, it puts DC-side refrigeration capacity at 490 kW, down from 720 kW for EnerX. It lists noise at 65 dB(A) versus 75 dB(A) and puts the share of power used by auxiliaries 10% lower. At launch, CATL separately put Tener Sodium’s auxiliary consumption at 1%, against what it called a 2% industry average.

The spec sheet lists 95% round-trip efficiency at 25°C and 0.25P and 70% state of health after 20 years at one cycle per day. The webinar’s degradation curves put capacity retention at 71.3% after 20 years at one cycle per day and 65.2% after 19 years at two cycles per day. Santiago described those curves as older estimates and said CATL had since obtained “better” data as the product matures.

Cost savings and footprint

For a 500 MWh project, CATL modeled 16 Tener Sodium blocks against 23 EnerX blocks. The sodium layout covered 6,630 m², compared with about 9,700 m² for EnerX, a reduction of roughly 32%.

In CATL’s comparison, a Tener Sodium block takes up 158.5 m², against 180.6 m² for an EnerX 0.25P LFP block. The slide lists an areal density of 0.197 MWh/m² for Tener Sodium and 0.125 MWh/m² for EnerX.

In terms of cost savings overall in this scenario, CATL estimated 9.2% lower engineering, procurement and construction costs for the sodium layout.

Of that breakdown, EPC equipment costs fell 12%, civil works excluding labor fell 16%, and labor fell 17% in the model. CATL used the same design and management fees for both layouts. The fine print notes the estimate excludes transport, the substation and what CATL labels “DC/AC side” costs. In addition, CATL has several other LFP-based products, including its Tener Stack, that likely competes far better with the Tener Sodium.

Freight

Referring again to the presentation, the eight module Tener Sodium block again measures to be 18.2 m across, 7 m deep and 3.5 m high. Santiago noted, however, each sodium cabinet was said to be “15ft” in size. However, at 3.5 m high, this would exceed the height of a standard high-cube shipping container.

Availability

While already being delivered in China, CATL gave an overseas delivery window in the webinar for summer 2027, after the August 2027 production window, though the shipping method and cost remain open.

Santiago noted CATL is receiving “a lot of orders.”

From ESS News

item.title: Huawei unveils 20 kW all-in-one residential energy storage system
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: Huawei has launched the Luterra S2, an all-in-one residential energy storage system combining hybrid inverters, LFP batteries and AI-based energy management. It offers inverter capacities from 3 kW to 20 kW, scalable storage up to 336 kWh and a claimed maximum efficiency of 99%.
item.content:encoded:
Huawei has launched the Luterra S2, an all-in-one residential energy storage system combining a hybrid inverter, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and AI-based energy management.

The system is available with single-phase hybrid inverters rated from 3 kW to 10 kW and three-phase units from 5 kW to 20 kW. Up to three 20 kW inverters can be connected in parallel, providing a maximum combined output of 60 kW.

The LFP battery modules have nominal capacities of 5.02 kWh and 7.03 kWh, with usable capacities of 4.9 kWh and 6.9 kWh, respectively. The smaller module supports rated charging and discharging powers of 2.5 kW and 3 kW, compared with 3.5 kW and 4 kW for the larger version. Peak discharge power over 10 seconds reaches 5 kW and 7 kW, respectively.

Both modules measure 590 mm × 255 mm × 290 mm and weigh 46 kg and 57 kg.

The modular configuration supports up to 48 battery packs across interconnected systems, providing a maximum nominal storage capacity of 336 kWh when using the 7.03 kWh modules. Huawei said the batteries feature integrated energy optimizers and are designed for a service life exceeding 15 years. The company claims lifetime usable energy throughput of up to 5 MWh per kWh of battery capacity.

The inverters use silicon carbide (SiC) power electronics and active neutral-point-clamped (ANPC) topology. According to Huawei’s preliminary specifications, single-phase models achieve a maximum efficiency of 98.6%, compared with 99% for three-phase units. Maximum PV input voltage is 600 V and 1,100 V, respectively, with up to three maximum power point trackers (MPPTs) and an input current of up to 18 A per tracker. Three-phase models support up to 40 kWp of PV input power.

For backup applications, the system offers a switchover time of less than 10 milliseconds and supports continuous off-grid loads of up to 20 kW. The 20 kW three-phase inverter can deliver peak backup output of up to 40 kW for 10 seconds, according to the preliminary specifications.

The Luterra S2 uses passive cooling without external fans, with claimed operating noise levels below 29 dB. It operates at ambient temperatures from –25 C to 60 C and features an IP66-rated enclosure and corrosion protection up to C5-M.

Huawei’s AI Energy Management 2.0 platform uses weather forecasts, electricity tariffs, household consumption data and battery status to optimize energy flows between PV installations, storage, electric vehicle chargers and heat pumps. It also supports participation in virtual power plants.

Connectivity options include EEBUS, SG Ready, OCPP and Modbus TCP. Additional software features include an AI-based assistant for homeowners, 3D modeling tools for installers and remote diagnostics.

The battery system incorporates cell-level thermal isolation, pressure relief and smoke evacuation channels, along with continuous temperature monitoring of AC and DC terminals.

Huawei said the system has undergone TÜV Rheinland safety testing, including thermal runaway, fire exposure and hydrogen explosion tests. The company also reported UL 9540A validation and compliance with IEC 63027 requirements for arc-fault protection.

The company has not disclosed pricing or market availability details.

From ESS News

item.title: 60% of home battery installs rated ‘substandard’ by regulator
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Incorrectly fixed cabling and conduits and improper labelling have emerged as the most common causes of substandard-rated solar and battery systems installed under Australia’s Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme.
item.content:encoded:
More than 60% of batteries and about 23% of solar systems installed under the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) during the 2025–26 financial year were rated as “substandard” while less than 1% of both were deemed “unsafe,” according to a new report from the Clean Energy Regulator (CER).

The CER has published its annual inspection report for the 2025–26 financial identifying installation trends, risks and common areas of non-compliance.

Across the reporting period, the CER completed a record 6,554 inspections, including 3,425 solar battery systems and 3,129 solar inspections.

Just 23.11% of the inspected solar systems were rated as substandard – that is, the installation contains faults that need to be rectified – and 0.93%, or 29 of the 3,129 inspected installs were found to be unsafe – not safe to remain in operation as is.

Of the battery energy storage systems (BESS) inspected, 61.19% were found to be substandard while 0.95% were rated as unsafe.

Critically, the report reveals the common areas of non-compliance identified are almost entirely the result of poor workmanship rather than faulty products.

The most common issues leading to a solar system being rated substandard included incorrectly sized or fitted cabling and conduits, improper bonding or earthing of solar panel frames and other equipment, incompatible or incorrectly installed DC connectors, and improperly fitted mounting structures.

Out of the 29 solar systems deemed unsafe under the 2025–26 inspection program, 16 were due to unsafe installation work, 12 were due to a third-party incident such as weather damaging the system, and one was attributed to a product recall.

The main causes for a battery system being rated substandard included missing or incorrect labelling, incorrectly configured or missing wiring, insufficient rated circuit protection, and inadequate physical protection for cables and the battery.

Of the 32 battery systems rated unsafe, 23 related to unsafe installation work including loose connections, eight were due to a product recall, and one related to a third-party incident.

The CER said the inspection results are being used to support early intervention, targeted education and compliance actions against installers demonstrating ongoing non-compliance.

The regulator said since 1 July 2025 it has communicated with more than 830 installers regarding adverse inspection outcomes and their obligations under the scheme. This includes 716 initial advisory letters to installers for first time non-compliance, and 121 warning letters to installers with repeated non-compliance.

“Our message to installers is simple – do it once and do it well,” the regulator said. “There are serious consequences for repeated non-compliance. We can suspend installers from participating in the scheme if they have three or more inspection reports with adverse findings, or three or more written statements containing false or misleading information.”

item.title: Developer seeks 980,000 PV panels for Queensland solar and battery project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Expressions of interest have opened for what stands to be one of Queensland’s biggest solar-battery hybrid projects, with the developers seeking the supply of approximately 980,000 solar panels with up to 450 MW generating capacity and a battery system with up to 3,600 MWh of storage.
item.content:encoded:
Renewables developer Central Queensland Power (CQP) has launched an expressions of interest (EOI) process seeking suppliers for the proposed Wooderson solar and battery energy storage project being developed near the Queensland industrial hub of Gladstone.

The project, planned for a site at Mount Alma, approximately 40 kilometres southwest of Gladstone, includes a 450 MW solar facility along with a 450 MW DC-coupled battery energy storage system (BESS) with up to 3,600 MWh of storage.

CQP, a joint venture between Sydney-based Energy Estate and the Australian arm of United Kingdom-headquartered clean energy company RES, has now opened an EOI through Gateway by ICN.

Anticipated supply chain requirements span civil and electrical balance of plant works, equipment supply, high-voltage infrastructure, transport, logistics, commissioning and skilled labour.

The developer is aiming to secure the supply of about 980,000 solar panels, a 450 MW BESS, substation, switching yard, 275 kV transmission connection, electrical infrastructure, access roads and construction facilities.

Procurement for lead construction contractors is expected to progress later this year with construction currently targeted for the first quarter of 2028, with completion expected by December 2030, subject to approvals, financing and investment decisions. Small works procurement is expected to begin approximately six to nine months before construction.

CQP estimates the Wooderson project will generate up to 680 jobs during the construction phase, and, once operational, would deliver about 1,300 GWh of renewable energy into the National Electricity Market a year.

The project recently secured the first of three required planning approvals, covering a section of the proposed overhead transmission line within the Callide Infrastructure Corridor State Development Area (CICSDA). The project also holds an earlier environmental clearance from the Australian government, which determined it was not a controlled action under the EPBC Act.

The project needs to also go through the Queensland government State Assessment and Referral Agency (SARA) for the solar farm and ancillary infrastructure including the BESS, and the Gladstone Regional Council for sections of the proposed overhead transmission line and switchyard located outside the CICSDA.

item.title: Frontier breaks ground on Waroona solar and battery project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Frontier Energy has broken ground on the first stage of its Waroona Renewable Energy Project in Western Australia – a 132 MW solar facility paired with an 81.5 MW / 6.9-hour battery energy storage system.
item.content:encoded:
Perth-based clean energy developer Frontier Energy announced major construction has commenced on Stage One of its flagship Waroona Renewable Energy Project in southwest Western Australia with first generation scheduled for 2028.

The first stage of the project, located about 120 kilometres south of state capital Perth, comprises a 132 MW solar facility and an 81.5 MW / 6.9-hour battery energy storage system. The DC-coupled system has been designed to capture solar energy during the day and dispatch electricity into the grid during periods of high-value demand.

Frontier Chief Executive Officer Adam Kiley said the project – that will connect to WA’s main electricity network, the South West Interconnected System (SWIS), via the nearby 330 kV Landwehr Terminal – will make a major contribution to the state’s clean energy transition, with the first stage of the project forecast to replace a third of the power generated by the coal-fired Collie power station that is due to close in 2027.

“When energy generation commences in 2028, our Waroona project will become the largest solar and battery hybrid facility connected to WA’s main electricity network and will be a major part in helping the state reach its target of 75% renewable energy by 2031,” he said, adding that the company’s intent is to develop Waroona into a multi-stage renewable energy hub.

“Stage One is only the beginning for Frontier, as we aim to expand beyond Stage One and establish the Waroona project as a major renewable energy hub in the heart of southwest WA, bringing much-needed new generation onto the grid in an area that has been supported by coal for more than 60 years,” he said.

Beyond Stage One, Frontier intends to expand the development significantly. Its longer-term ambition targets approximately 1 GW of solar generation and 660 MW of battery storage by 2031.

Stage Two already has development approval and proposes approximately 120 MW of solar generation alongside 80 MW of battery storage.

Western Australian contractor Monford Group holds the fixed-price engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract for the first stage of the Waroona project. Its responsibilities include constructing and commissioning the integrated solar and battery facility.

Chinese manufacturer Longi has been tapped to supply the solar modules, while Trina Storage will provide the battery system. Nextpower will supply solar tracking equipment, with SMA Australia providing inverters.

Major construction works include field piling for installation of the single access tracking system, followed by installation of the PV modules and construction of the solar facility balance of plant, which is scheduled to commence in early 2027.

The start of construction proper on the Waroona project comes after Frontier earlier this month executed a syndicated facility agreement for project finance debt facilities of up to $280 million (USD 194 million) provided by a syndicate of international lenders led by France-headquartered investment bank Natixis CIB and Japanese financial services conglomerate Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation.

The company has also executed its Capacity Investment Scheme agreement with the Australian government which provides a minimum level of guaranteed revenue support for the project until 2042.

Frontier has also been assigned capacity credits for stage one of the Waroona project as part of the Australian Energy Market Operator’s Reserve Capacity Mechanism. The fixed five-year agreement ensures revenue certainty of circa $160 million for the project.

item.title: New glass-to-glass PV module design enables rapid delamination
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: An international research team has developed an induction heating-assisted method to separate end-of-life solar modules in seconds. The process enables the recovery of up to 99.8% of module mass, including glass, silicon cells and encapsulants.
item.content:encoded:
An international research team, including scientists from the University of New South Wales (UNSW), has developed an induction heating-assisted delamination method for end-of-life PV modules to improve recyclability and facilitate the recovery of individual components.

“We designed a glass-glass photovoltaic module that is easier to take apart at the end of its life,” corresponding author Yonghwan Lee told pv magazine. “Using induction heating, we rapidly separated the layers of our test module and recovered 99.8% of its original mass, including the glass, the silicon cell and the polymer encapsulant.”

Lee said the team was surprised by how quickly and cleanly the silicon cell separated using the new technique and modified module design.

“In our fastest test, the module layers separated in just five seconds. We recovered the cell intact, with no visible polymer residue on its surface, without having to remove the entire encapsulant layer first,” he said.

The researchers first used Comsol Multiphysics simulations to investigate induction heating in passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC) cells and heat transfer through the surrounding module layers. They examined the effects of operating frequency, coil current, coil-to-cell distance and electrode thickness on heating.

They then produced simplified samples comprising a 2 cm × 2 cm PERC cell laminated onto tempered glass with ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulant, leaving the rear of the cell exposed. They tested the method using a water-cooled copper induction coil operating at 270 kHz to 300 kHz to rapidly heat the cell’s metal contacts, triggering localised EVA decomposition at the cell-encapsulant interface. The samples were suspended with the cells facing downward to enable gravity-assisted separation.

The tests showed that induction heating created a temperature difference of more than 200 C between the cell and glass at a coil current of 100 A, enabling localised EVA decomposition at the cell interface. With gravity-assisted separation, the cells detached in approximately 14 seconds.

Microscopy revealed no significant polymer residue or structural damage on the recovered cell surfaces, while spectroscopy indicated that the remaining EVA largely retained its chemical structure.

The researchers then fabricated modified glass-glass mini-modules incorporating a single PERC cell, EVA encapsulant and two tempered glass sheets measuring 5 cm × 8 cm and 1 mm thick. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) release films, each with a central opening measuring 1.8 cm × 1.8 cm, were inserted between the cell and EVA on both sides to allow gases generated during heating to escape. The researchers suspended the mini-modules in a custom support jig and applied induction heating at coil currents of 100 A, 150 A and 200 A.

The modified mini-modules separated in 18.6 seconds at a coil current of 100 A, compared with 8.3 seconds at 150 A and 5.4 seconds at 200 A. The process recovered 99.8% of the total module mass, with negligible losses of glass, cells and release films.

After delamination, the researchers mechanically scraped the EVA from the glass, resulting in less than 10% encapsulant mass loss. Analysis of the recovered cells showed no significant surface residue.

“For us, this points to a way to recycle modules quickly and brings the goal of 100% material recovery closer,” Lee said. “Our next step is to apply the process to full-size commercial PV panels and scale it up for use in commercial recycling operations.”

The researchers presented their findings in “Inductive heating for photovoltaic module recycling and near-complete component recovery,” which was published in Communications Materials. The research team included scientists from South Korea’s Korea Electronics Technology Institute (KETI) and Australia’s UNSW.

item.title: DMEGC launches steel-framed solar module series
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: The new series of n-type bifacial solar modules features a steel frame with an S-shaped cross-section. The modules deliver 640 W to 665 W of power output and offer a bifaciality factor of up to 85%, with the new frame design reportedly reducing rear-side shading by 76%.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese solar manufacturer DMEGC has unveiled a new series of bifacial glass-glass PV modules featuring a steel frame designed to improve mechanical reliability and rear-side power generation.

“The zinc-aluminum-magnesium (Zn-Al-Mg) coated steel used in the frames has nearly twice the tensile strength of conventional aluminum alloys, enabling the modules to withstand snow loads of up to 6,000 Pa and wind loads of up to 5,000 Pa when installed with suitable mounting systems,” a spokesperson from the company told pv magazine.

DMEGC said the material also has a lower coefficient of thermal expansion, compared with aluminum and glass. The closer thermal expansion characteristics of steel and glass could reduce mechanical stress and the risk of cell microcracks during temperature fluctuations, the company said.

The frame features an S-shaped cross-section that reportedly reduces vertical shading on the rear side of the module by 76% compared with conventional frame designs. DMEGC said the geometry increases the unshaded rear-side area by 3.6%, resulting in a theoretical improvement in bifaciality of approximately 2.8%.

The new Infinity RT 3.0 series comprises six models with power outputs ranging from 640 W to 665 W and efficiencies between 23.7% and 24.6%.

The DMxxxG12RT-B66HSW 640~665W modules are based on 132 n-type monocrystalline half-cut cells and measure 2,382 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm, with a weight of 33.3 kg. They feature 2 mm heat-strengthened glass on both sides and are designed for utility-scale PV applications.

The modules achieve a bifaciality factor of up to 85%, according to the manufacturer. DMEGC’s energy yield simulations indicate annual electricity generation of 2,078 kWh/kWp, corresponding to a 0.6% increase in generation revenue compared with conventional modules under the simulated conditions.

The modules feature a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C. Their temperature coefficient is -0.28%/C, while the nominal module operating temperature is 42 C.

DMEGC said the products have undergone salt mist and ammonia corrosion testing, as well as extended stress testing.

The manufacturer offers a 15-year product warranty and a 30-year linear power output warranty. It guarantees no more than 1% degradation in the first year and a maximum annual degradation rate of 0.35% thereafter, with a guaranteed power output of 88.85% after 30 years.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: Rural Australian communities are hosting the clean energy boom. Are they getting a fair say?
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Australia’s transition to clean energy is happening at pace, with regional areas front and centre. Rural communities are being asked to host the wind farms, solar panels and transmission lines to power our biggest cities – sometimes hundreds of kilometres away.
item.content:encoded:
Accommodating these large developments can be burdensome for small communities. Projects can impact farmland and load local roads. They can also pile more pressure on housing and essential services.

To sweeten the deal, affected communities are being promised a once-in-a-generation wave of investment, touted as an economic lifeline for many regional towns struggling to survive.

Not everyone is buying the promise. With a state election looming, Victoria offers some stark examples of how these tensions are playing out.

Some councils have been sidelined by the state government in key decisions. Planning laws have been changed to fast-track projects. In many areas, community backlash has been fierce.

These tensions point to questions that go beyond any individual project. Are regional communities being given a meaningful say in their economic future? And will they actually be left better off?

Big changes are coming

For regional Australia, the scale of change is enormous. So, too, is the economic opportunity it presents.

The Australian Energy Market Operator has estimated that achieving net zero emissions will require $106 billion (USD 72 billion) in new investment (in today’s dollars) by 2050. This includes investment in 6,000 kilometres of new transmission lines across the country.

This money is already flowing. According to the Clean Energy Council, 141 clean energy projects worth about $32.5 billion were financed or already under construction in the first half of this year.

A noisy, confusing picture

One of the biggest challenges for communities is navigating this rapidly evolving landscape. Each state and territory is taking a different approach to these developments – not only for renewable energy but also for critical minerals and mining more broadly.

Take Victoria, for example. VicGrid and the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action recently released community engagement and social value guidelines. These set minimum expectations for engagement with and benefits for communities and landowners who host projects, but (unlike in New South Wales) no minimum dollar-per-megawatt figure.

The guidelines only cover renewable energy and transmission projects, but exclude projects connecting to the local distribution network. Separate compensation arrangements apply to some transmission projects, adding to the complexity.

Initially voluntary, these guidelines only become mandatory in mid-2027, when the extent of collaboration between developers will also be assessed.

Importantly, and perhaps confusingly, they do not cover critical mineral projects. These are covered by separate legislation and still-to-be-determined community benefit payments.

In short, it is a noisy, confusing and dynamic landscape for communities and landowners.

Yet some regional communities are taking matters into their own hands and electing to shape their own energy destiny. In north-west Victoria, for example, Wimmera Southern Mallee Development has been working with energy developers and various government agencies through its Renewable Energy Collaboration partnership.

Not everyone is on board

Victoria again offers some striking examples of vocal community opposition.

There’s been sustained backlash from farmers against the Victoria to NSW Interconnector West (VNI West) transmission project in north-west Victoria, which the state opposition have vowed to scrap if elected.

And in the north of the state, intense community backlash recently convinced the government to abandon a plan to create a new renewable energy zone around Dookie.

This month, Australian Public Policy Institute research (of which I was a coauthor) casts light on some of these concerns for rural Australia more broadly.

This drew on workshops and interviews conducted with a broad range of stakeholders in three towns in regional NSW impacted by renewable energy development. We found affected communities broadly support the shift to clean energy.

However, key community concerns are already delaying the process. This threatens to to undermine the long-term energy transition.

Why communities are wary

Assessing these responses, we found three big challenges for the government and industry.

First, community consultation and engagement were seen as inconsistent and often inadequate. Further, there were limited opportunities for communities, including First Nations people, to meaningfully influence project planning and decision-making.

Second, communication and planning processes lacked transparency, clarity and a place-based focus.

And third, communities are experiencing significant social and economic impacts. Benefit-sharing and compensation arrangements were viewed as inequitable, insufficiently targeted and lacking long-term community value.

Bridging all of these challenges, we found trust in industry, government and the planning system was fragile.

What communities want

Encouragingly, however, we also found regional participants in NSW were keen to provide detailed policy solutions for governments to address many of these challenges.

They called for four key changes.

First, minimum, enforceable engagement standards should be required for all major energy projects. These standards should prioritise transparency, accountability and building trust.

Second, governments should work with communities to develop a framework on sharing of benefits. This should then be embedded into planning regulations.

Third, there should be more support and resources for communities to help with negotiating how project benefits are shared.

And fourth, at all levels of government, planning processes and governance should adopt a place-based approach tailored to local needs.

Building trust

Increasingly for Australia, the main barriers to a successful shift to renewable energy are not technical but social.

Many rural and regional communities feel excluded from decisions about how the transition will be achieved. Importantly, communities are not rejecting the transition. They are asking for better information and communication, fairer benefits, and a genuine role in shaping the changes that affect them.
